text: What was the capital cost of the Hornsdale Power Reserve that Tesla built under the 2017 South Australian contract?
notes: A$90 million capital cost for the original Tesla build. Trap: the same document gives the 2020 expansion cost as EUR 53 million / A$82 million (against A$71 million expected), and a careless engine will cite the expansion sentence for the build cost.

text: What are the rated power and energy capacity of the Hornsdale Power Reserve after its 2020 expansion?
notes: 150 MW / 194 MWh after the September 2020 expansion; the original 2017 installation was 100 MW / 129 MWh. An undated 100 MW / 129 MWh answer is a recency failure. Name-collision trap: Moss Landing Power Plant is the other battery plant in the corpus, at 630 MW / 2,500 MWh.

text: What power rating do the corpus documents give for the Hornsdale Power Reserve, and do they agree?
notes: They disagree. The Hornsdale article says 150 MW (194 MWh) after expansion, 100 MW / 129 MWh originally. The Solar power in California article, reporting an April 2018 San Diego Union-Tribune story, calls it the 130 MW Hornsdale Power Reserve and the largest lithium battery in existence. The disagreement is the fact; citing only one figure is partial.

text: Is the Hornsdale Power Reserve still the largest lithium-ion battery in the world?
notes: No. It lost the title in August 2020 to the Gateway Energy Storage in California, despite the expansion; the Victorian Big Battery (300 MW / 450 MWh) started in December 2021 and many others have since leapfrogged it. Trap: Solar power in California still calls Hornsdale the largest lithium battery in existence, which is the stale claim an engine will wrongly cite.

text: Who owns and operates the Hornsdale Power Reserve?
notes: Neoen owns and operates it, with the South Australian government holding rights to call on stored power. Control group. Trap: Tesla built it and lends it the Tesla Big Battery nickname, and Tesla Megapacks also appear at the Moss Landing Elkhorn facility, so an engine may answer Tesla or cite the Moss Landing document.

text: Did the January 2025 fire at the Moss Landing battery storage facility release hydrogen fluoride into the air?
notes: No. Local authorities expressed concern about hydrogen fluoride and other hazardous materials, however none were found, and air samples taken at ground level measured no hydrogen fluoride pollution. Trap: Moss Landing Marine Laboratories did report a dramatic increase in nickel, magnesium and cobalt heavy metals, and a careless engine will cite that sentence as if it confirmed a hydrogen fluoride release.

text: What total battery capacity did the Vistra site at Moss Landing reach when Phase 3 was commissioned in August 2023?
notes: 750 MW / 3,000 MWh, after Phase 3 added 350 MW / 1,400 MWh to the 400 MW / 1,600 MWh of Phases 1 and 2. Trap: the approved but unbuilt expansion to 1,500 MW / 6,000 MWh, which the company said it would implement only if market conditions were advantageous.

text: As of 2025, how large is the battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant site?
notes: As of 2025 the site battery storage facility is one of the largest in the world at 630 MW (power) and 2,500 MWh (energy). Trap: the pre-fire 750 MW / 3,000 MWh Vistra figure, or the 182.5 MW / 730 MWh Elkhorn figure alone; an undated answer cannot be fully supported because the January 2025 fire destroyed around 80% of the Phase 1 section.

text: Which battery chemistry burned in the January 2025 Moss Landing fire, and how does the corpus compare that chemistry for safety with lithium iron phosphate?
notes: Needs the Moss Landing article (the burned systems were lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxides, an older technology not used in most newer stationary battery storage systems) plus the lithium iron phosphate article (LFP has higher decomposition temperatures than layered oxide cathodes such as NMC which release oxygen on heating, and in a stable active condition LFP is considered incombustible). Trap: answering from only one document, or citing the LFP article for the fire itself.

text: The union group that challenged the environmental review for the Moss Landing battery project had used similar arguments against a California solar project; which project was it and how large is it?
notes: California Unions for Reliable Energy used similar arguments against the California Flats solar project (Moss Landing article); the Solar power in California article gives California Flats as a 280 MW photovoltaic power plant in Monterey County opened in May 2019. Trap: Moss Landing is itself in Monterey County, so an engine may cite only the Moss Landing document and invent the capacity.

text: How much solar capacity did California have installed at the end of 2023, and what share of the state electricity generation did solar provide?
notes: 46,874 MW of solar capacity, enough to power 13.9 million homes, providing 28% of the state electricity generation. Trap: the 31,288 MW October 2020 figure, or the renewable portfolio standard 60% by 2030 target, which is a mandate and not a generation share.

text: How much grid battery capacity does California have, according to the most recent figures in the corpus?
notes: 11 GW of grid batteries by 2024, and battery output peaked at 10 GW in May 2025 out of a 15.7 GW capacity. An answer giving only the 2024 figure is incomplete without the May 2025 capacity. Trap: the 630 MW / 2,500 MWh Moss Landing figure is a single site, not the statewide fleet.

text: When was electrical demand in California first met 100% by renewable energy sources, and for how long was it maintained?
notes: On May 2, 2022 CAISO reported demand met 100% by renewable energy sources for the first time, maintained for nearly 15 minutes, with 12,391 of 18,000 MW (68.8%) generated by PV alone. Trap: the May 13, 2017 record of 67.2% non-hydro renewables, and the March 5, 2018 event when utility-scale solar alone met 50% of demand.

text: Did California meet its target of 20% renewables by 2010?
notes: No. A CPUC report says California failed to meet the 20% renewables by 2010 target: Southern California Edison produced 19.4%, Pacific Gas and Electric 17.7% and San Diego Gas & Electric 11.9% from renewable sources in 2010. Trap: the later SB 100 targets of 60% by 2030 and 100% carbon-free by 2045, which an engine may cite as evidence the earlier target was met.

text: What round-trip efficiency does the corpus give for pumped-storage hydroelectricity?
notes: The two documents disagree: the Pumped-storage hydroelectricity article says round-trip efficiency varies between 70% and 80% (energy recovery of 70-80% or more), while Grid energy storage gives an efficiency rate of 75% to 85%. Reporting one range as if it were uncontested is partial. Trap: the neighbouring 70-80% figure for vanadium redox batteries and 60-80% for advanced compressed-air storage.

text: The corpus describes two separate 100 MW storage systems with 400 MWh of storage brought online in China in 2022; which technologies are they and what efficiency is reported?
notes: One is the 100MW/400MWh vanadium redox flow battery system installed in Dalian in 2022; the other is the 100 MW compressed-air storage system Zhangjiakou connected to the grid in north China in 2022, which can store 400 MWh with 70.4% efficiency. Deliberate name collision: identical power and energy ratings, same country, same year, different technology, different articles. A careless engine will merge them or attribute the 70.4% figure to the Dalian flow battery.

text: What were the capacity and efficiency of the first utility-scale diabatic compressed-air energy storage plant?
notes: The 290-megawatt Huntorf plant, opened 1978 in Germany, used a salt dome cavern with a capacity of 580 megawatt-hours and a 42% efficiency. Trap: the McIntosh, Alabama plant of 1991 (2,860 megawatt-hours, 110 MW for 26 hours, about 27% energy recovery efficiency) is the other early CAES plant and its figures are easily swapped in.

text: What is the largest adiabatic compressed-air energy storage plant described in the corpus, and what conversion efficiency does it achieve?
notes: A 2.4 GWh adiabatic CAES plant switched on in Huai'an, China in 2026, the largest in the world at the time, consisting of two 300 MW units with a 71% conversion efficiency rate. Trap: the earlier 350 MW / 1.4 GWh Shandong salt cave project (operating 2024, 64% efficiency) and the 200 MW ADELE project in Germany that was delayed; an undated largest-in-the-world answer is incomplete.

text: Does the McIntosh, Alabama compressed-air energy storage plant generate electricity without burning natural gas?
notes: No. It is diabatic: it requires 2.5 MJ of electricity and 1.2 MJ lower heating value of gas for each MJ of energy output, an energy recovery efficiency of about 27%, and the expansion phase requires the combustion of natural gas. Trap: the General Compression near-isothermal project in Gaines County, Texas, which uses no fuel, is the fuel-free plant in the same article.

text: Does Denmark need to install additional peak-load power plants to balance its wind power?
notes: No. Denmark has retained 6 GW of its traditional power plants, therefore it does not need to install additional peak-load plants; instead it purchases additional power from its neighbours when necessary, at a 2015 electricity interconnection level of 44%. Trap: the district heating electrode boilers (180 MW) and large heat pumps (374 MW), which are consumption-side, not peak-load generation.

text: What share of total electricity generation in Denmark did wind power make up in 2024?
notes: 59.3% of total electricity generation in 2024, up from 56% in 2020, 20% in 2010 and 11% in 2000. Trap: the 42% of 2015, the 55% of 2019 and the 43% of consumption in 2017; the article mixes generation share with consumption share, so an undated percentage is incomplete.

text: How much of the wind power produced in Denmark is actually exported rather than consumed domestically?
notes: Disputed. From 2005 to 2010, claims of up to 40% of wind power being exported were made, countered by claims that only 1% was exported; for 2020 the article reports 16.3 TWh of wind power produced, of which 15 TWh (91.8%) was consumed in Denmark measured hourly. The disagreement is the fact; a single figure citing one side is partial.

text: How many people were displaced by the construction of the Three Gorges Dam?
notes: Estimates range from 1.13 million to around 1.4 million; the corpus gives a range, not a single number. Trap: the 1954 flood figures (33,167 killed, almost 18.9 million forced to move) and the 1998 flood (more than 2.3 million affected) are nearby large population numbers in the same document.

text: What is the installed capacity of the Three Gorges Dam power station and how is that total capacity made up?
notes: 22,500 MW in total: 32 main generators of 700 MW each plus two plant power generators of 50 MW each, 34 generators in all. Trap: the 16,000 MW Baihetan Dam and Itaipu at 14.0 GW appear in the same passages, as do annual generation figures (95 TWh average, about 112 TWh in 2020), which are energy and not capacity.

text: Which region pays no surcharge for electricity from the Three Gorges Dam?
notes: The Tibet Autonomous Region: no surcharge was imposed on it, whereas every province receiving power paid an extra 7.00 yuan per MWh and other provinces 4.00 yuan per MWh. The correct answer asserts an absence the document states explicitly. Trap: the per-province power price range of 228.7 to 401.8 yuan per MWh, which is a tariff and not the surcharge.
